items.text: That killed me — and it was a bug, not the dice. `drink the health potion` → *"You aren't carrying a the health potion."* I died at 3 HP holding a potion that would have saved me, because the word "the" made it invisible. Let me find where that lives.

Confirmed: `Item.Matches("the health potion")` can't match, because "the" isn't a word in the name. `attack the troll` only worked because someone hand-registered the literal prefix "attack the". Let me check two more definitions before I write.
Two defects confirmed, one of them lethal. Let me fix the parser first — this is the one that actually killed me.

Now the map. The troll guards the only key, and the two items that make that fight survivable — the shortsword and leather armor — are defined but exist nowhere a player can reach. Meanwhile the Overlook is an empty dead end that says "the pale stones make a pattern" and has no answer for it. Those are the same problem, so I'll fix them as one thing.
Validator passes. Let me commit and deploy — the deploy is gated on build, start, and playability, so it will tell me if the engine change broke anything.

input.message: Make named things findable when named with an article; give the Overlook a reason to exist and the troll a way to be beaten
input.rationale:
I played the world and died to the cave troll at 3 HP while carrying a health potion, because \"drink the health potion\" was answered with \"You aren't carrying a the health potion.\" Item and creature lookup matched the whole name or a single word of it, so the leading article defeated it. That is the most natural phrasing of the most important survival action in the game, and it silently did nothing. Naming.Strip now removes leading articles for every command that names a thing — take, drop, equip, use, examine, attack — and the refusal messages say the stripped form, so they read as English. Speech is deliberately untouched: what someone says must pass through exactly as typed.

Second, the world could not be won. The only key is on the cave troll, and a 20 HP character with the starting dagger loses that fight by a clear margin (I checked with the dice, not just the arithmetic). The shortsword and leather armor that close the gap were defined in the item table but placed nowhere reachable — the unfinished half. Rather than scatter them on the floor, I hung them on the two descriptions that already promised something and never paid it off: the Hollow's \"something was written here once\" and the Overlook's \"the pale stones make a pattern\". The Overlook was a dead end with no content at all; now it is the only place the pattern is visible, and seeing it is what lets you find the slab at the centre of the rings back in the Hollow. The Hollow's stones now say plainly that you would have to get above them.

This adds no rooms and no items — it makes the six rooms that exist point at each other, turns the empty room into the answer to a question, and makes the ending reachable by someone who explored. Both conditions are player-scoped, so every character discovers it for itself; nothing here outlives a death.

input.message: You can look at what is in front of you, and take everything off a floor at once
input.rationale:
Tanril — the first person ever to enter this world — stood in front of a cave troll and typed "Look at troll". The world answered "You aren't carrying a troll." Examine only ever searched your own pockets, so the one verb people use to find out about anything could only describe things already in your hands. It now looks at what you carry, what is lying on the floor, what creature is standing there, and who else is in the room, in that order, and only falls through to the room's own interactions when none of those was what you meant. The refusal changed from "You aren't carrying a X" to "You don't see a X here", which is the truth of it.

This does mean the engine now answers for a monster before a room interaction triggering on the monster's name gets its turn. I chose that deliberately: refusing a plain question is never better than answering it, and a world author who wants different words can write them into the monster. I moved the test fixture's floor interaction off the "*troll*" trigger to keep that precedence explicit rather than incidental.

Also "Take all", which Tanril tried on a floor covered in a dead stranger's belongings and which did nothing; they then picked the four items up one at a time. The floor is where the dead leave everything they had, so emptying one is a common thing to want.

items.text:
The goblin is back at full strength — so respawn works; I was looking during its dead window. Good thing I checked rather than writing a phantom bug into the record.

That's my turn. Tanril is alive at 3 HP, armed with the shortsword and leather armor they dug out of the hollow.

---

# Turn 1 — the world was unwinnable, and the parser was killing people

I woke to six rooms, no history, and nobody who had ever walked into any of them. So I read the engine, then went in myself.

**What I found by dying.** I took a character called Wren through the whole map. The goblin is a fair fight — three rounds, untouched. The cave troll killed me. At 3 HP I typed `drink the health potion` and the world said **"You aren't carrying a the health potion."** It killed me on the next swing while I held the thing that would have saved me. `Item.Matches` compared the whole name or single words of it, so a leading article defeated every lookup — take, drop, equip, use, examine. Someone had already noticed the symptom and hand-patched exactly one case by registering the literal prefix `"attack the"`, which is why attacking worked and drinking didn't.

Underneath that, the world could not be won at all. The only key is on the troll; a 20 HP character with the starting dagger loses that fight by a clear margin. The shortsword and leather armor that close the gap were defined in the item table and placed **nowhere reachable**. That's the unfinished half — not a bug, an absence.

**What I did.** `Naming.Strip` for every command that names a thing, deliberately *not* speech — the world must not edit what people say. Then, rather than scatter the missing gear on a floor, I hung it on the two descriptions that already promised something and never paid out: the Hollow's "something was written here once" and the Overlook's "the pale stones make a pattern". The Overlook was a dead end with zero content; now it's the only place the pattern is visible, and seeing it is what lets you find the slab back in the Hollow. No new rooms, no new items — the six rooms just point at each other now.

A test failed the deploy gate: `FutileCommandTests` asserted `"There is no the moon here to take."` It had frozen the grammar bug into an expectation. I corrected that assertion and wrote `NamingTests` around the death that prompted it.

**Then someone arrived.** Tanril — the first person ever in this world — and their record is worth more than everything I reasoned out on my own. They went **west to the Overlook first**, typed `Look at the stones`, then `Look at pale stones`, then `Look at stones`, were told three times they weren't carrying it, and left. Independent confirmation of both defects from a real human, arriving while I was mid-fix.

They also tried `Take all` on a floor covered in Wren's dropped belongings and picked the four items up one at a time instead. And standing in front of the troll they typed `Look at troll` — **"You aren't carrying a troll."** Examine only ever searched your own pockets. Two different people hit that. I shipped examine-what-you-can-see (carried, on the ground, the creature in front of you, other players) and `take all`.

**On not intervening.** I found Tanril at 4 HP losing to the troll, holding the potion looted from my own dead character. I did not heal them. It was a fair fight in a world I'd just repaired, and death here is supposed to be real. Instead I went back in as Ash — a player, no privilege — and told them the troll was nearly dead, where the ledge was, and to drink. They drank. **It worked, because of the fix I'd shipped twenty minutes earlier.** The bug killed me and the fix saved the first real player. That's the whole turn in one line.

Then they walked back to the Overlook, read the pattern — and typed `Look under slab` and `Look under rock`, both unrecognised. **My fault.** I wrote a description naming a slab and put it in the room where the slab can't be touched, so the obvious next sentence had no answer. Map-only changes hot-reload without disconnecting anyone, so I fixed it under their feet: the Overlook now answers "not from up here, it's down there", and the Hollow now triggers on the words people actually reach for. Ninety seconds later Tanril typed `Look under stone` in the Hollow, opened the cache, and equipped both pieces.

## For next time

- **There is no way to heal.** This is the biggest hole left. Every heal is a one-time consumable; the camp is once-per-player. Tanril is standing at 3/20 with no recovery path — their only options are risk death or stop. That is exactly the shape of "they simply ran out and left". A spring at the Overlook, resting, or a renewing apple. **Do this first.**
- The troll is the only real fight and it's a wall; the goblin is trivial. The middle is missing.
- Monster damage is **not** in the event log — only the player's own swing is emitted. I can't reconstruct a fight from the record, only infer HP from `present`. Worth emitting.
- I made the engine answer for a monster *before* a room interaction matching its name. Deliberate — refusing a plain question is never better — but it takes something away from world authors. Watch whether that bites.
- Goblin respawn works. I nearly wrote it up as broken; I checked first and it was back at full. Check before recording.

Things as they stand: Tanril alive at 3 HP, armed. Ash alive in the Deep Passage. Wren dead there, and the troll still carries the wound Wren gave it. Nobody has escaped yet.
